stem: Two planets orbit the same star in nearly circular orbits. The orbital radius of planet B is four times that of planet A. What is the ratio of the orbital period of B to the orbital period of A?
explanation: Kepler’s third law gives T² ∝ r³ for bodies orbiting the same central mass; therefore (period of B)/(period of A) = 4^(3/2) = 8.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: A planet follows an elliptical orbit around a star. At which position does the planet move fastest?
options: At the point closest to the star
At the point furthest from the star
At the end of the minor axis
explanation: By Kepler’s second law, the radius vector sweeps out equal areas in equal times. The planet moves fastest when nearest the star.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: The masses of two small spheres are both doubled and the distance between their centres is tripled. What is the new gravitational force as a fraction of the original force?
explanation: F ∝ m₁m₂/r², so the force changes by a factor of (2×2)/3² = 4/9.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: Planet A has mass M and radius R. Planet B has mass 2M and radius 3R. What is the ratio of the gravitational field strength at B’s surface to that at A’s surface?
explanation: g = GM/R², so (field strength at B)/(field strength at A) = 2/(3²) = 2/9.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: The diagram shows the gravitational field around an isolated spherical mass M. Which statement is correct?
options: The field is directed away from M
The field has the same magnitude everywhere
The field is directed towards M
explanation: Gravitational force on a test mass is attractive, so the field lines point inward towards the mass. The spacing of lines indicates a weaker field further away.
diagramAlt: Eight radial gravitational field lines pointing inward towards a central spherical mass labelled M.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: A small satellite exerts a gravitational force of magnitude F on a much more massive planet. What force does the planet exert on the satellite?
options: F times the mass ratio, in the opposite direction
A smaller force, in the opposite direction
explanation: Newton’s third law requires equal and opposite forces, irrespective of the masses.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: The gravitational field strength at the surface of a spherical planet of radius R is g₀. What is the field strength at a height R above its surface?
explanation: The distance from the centre doubles from R to 2R. By the inverse-square law, g = g₀/4.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: Which quantity is constant for all planets orbiting the same star, to a good approximation?
explanation: Kepler’s third law states T²/r³ is constant for planets orbiting the same star, where r is the semimajor axis (or radius for a circular orbit).
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: Two planets have the same uniform density. Planet B has twice the radius of planet A. What is (field strength at B)/(field strength at A) at their surfaces?
explanation: Mass is proportional to density × R³; g = GM/R² ∝ ρR for uniform-density spheres. Hence the surface field doubles.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: A moon completes a circular orbit in period T at radius r. Another moon orbits the same planet at radius 9r. What is its orbital period?
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: Two point masses M and 4M are separated by distance 3d. At what distance from M, along the line between the masses, is the resultant gravitational field zero?
explanation: Between the masses GM/x² = G(4M)/(3d−x)², giving 3d−x = 2x and x = d.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: The gravitational potential at the surface of a spherical planet of radius R is −6.0 MJ kg⁻¹. What is the potential at a height 2R above the surface?
explanation: The distance from the centre is 3R; V = −GM/r, so the potential is one third its surface value: −2.0 MJ kg⁻¹.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: A small mass m is moved slowly from a distance 2R to 3R from a fixed point mass M. What is the work done by an external agent against gravity?
explanation: ΔU = −GMm/(3R) − (−GMm/(2R)) = +GMm/(6R). A slow controlled outward transfer requires this positive external work.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: A planet has radius R and gravitational field strength g at its surface. What is the escape speed from its surface, neglecting atmospheric drag?
explanation: escape speed = √(2GM/R) and g = GM/R², so escape speed = √(2gR).
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: The diagram shows gravitational potential V as a function of distance r from the centre of a spherical planet. How does the magnitude of the gravitational field change as r increases?
options: It decreases because the gradient becomes less steep
It is constant because V is always negative
It increases because V approaches zero
explanation: The field magnitude is |g| = |−dV/dr|. The graph becomes less steep with increasing r, so the magnitude of g decreases.
diagramAlt: Graph of negative gravitational potential increasing towards zero as distance from a planet increases; slope decreases in magnitude.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: A satellite in a circular orbit of radius r has orbital speed v around a planet. What is its speed in a circular orbit of radius 4r around the same planet?
explanation: orbital speed = √(GM/r). Multiplying the orbital radius by four halves the orbital speed.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: A satellite of mass m moves in a circular orbit of radius r around a planet of mass M. What is the total mechanical energy of the satellite–planet system?
explanation: K = GMm/(2r) from the circular-orbit condition, U = −GMm/r; hence total energy = −GMm/(2r).
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: A satellite is transferred from a circular orbit of radius r to a circular orbit of radius 2r around the same planet. What is the increase in total mechanical energy?
explanation: For circular orbits E = −GMm/(2r). The change is −GMm/(4r) − (−GMm/(2r)) = GMm/(4r).
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: Two isolated point masses, M and 9M, are separated by distance 8d, as shown. Where is the gravitational field strength zero?
explanation: Equate field magnitudes between the masses: GM/x² = 9GM/(8d−x)². Since 8d−x = 3x, x = 2d.
diagramAlt: Point masses M and 9M separated by distance 8d along a horizontal dashed line.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: At a point between two positive masses, the gravitational fields from the masses cancel. Which statement about the gravitational potential at this point is necessarily correct, taking zero at infinity?
options: The potential equals the potential of either mass alone
explanation: Gravitational potential is a scalar. Each positive mass contributes a negative potential, so their sum is negative even though the vector fields cancel.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: Which statement about gravitational equipotential surfaces is correct?
options: They are parallel to gravitational field lines
The gravitational force on a test mass acts tangentially to them
Work is needed to move a test mass along one equipotential
Gravitational field lines intersect equipotentials at right angles
explanation: The gravitational field is perpendicular to each equipotential surface; motion along one has ΔV = 0 and thus no work against gravity.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: Two isolated spherical planets have the same uniform density. Planet B has three times the radius of planet A. How does the magnitude of the potential at B’s surface compare with that at A’s surface?
options: It is one third as large
explanation: |surface potential magnitude| = GM/R and M ∝ ρR³, hence |surface potential magnitude| ∝ ρR². With equal density and three times the radius, magnitude increases by 9.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: The gravitational potential at a location outside a planet is −8.0 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. What is the minimum speed needed to escape from this location with zero final speed at infinity?
explanation: Energy conservation: (1/2)v² + V = 0, so v = √(−2V) = √(1.6 × 10⁷) = 4.0 × 10³ m s⁻¹.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: A satellite initially moves in a low circular orbit around Earth. Small atmospheric drag causes its orbit gradually to decay. Which change occurs to its orbital speed as it settles into a lower approximately circular orbit?
explanation: The lower circular orbit has smaller r and higher orbital speed v = √(GM/r), even though drag removes the satellite’s total mechanical energy.
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.

stem: A satellite of mass m starts at rest on the surface of a non-rotating spherical planet of mass M and radius R. Neglecting drag, what is the minimum energy that must be supplied to place it in a circular orbit of radius 2R?
explanation: Initially the satellite is at rest, so its energy is −GMm/R. In the circular orbit of radius 2R, its total energy is −GMm/(4R). The required energy input is the difference: 3GMm/(4R).
sourceNote: Original item aligned with the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025); teacher-supplied D.1 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme used only to benchmark style and challenge.
